lesson.title: Asymptote Analysis: Mapping the Places a Curve Never Quite Reaches
lesson.summary: Vertical, horizontal, and slant asymptotes each come from a different comparison, a zero denominator, a limit at infinity, or a mismatch in polynomial degree, and together they frame where a curve lives at its extremes.
lesson.body:
Asymptote analysis covers three distinct types, and each one comes from a different question, so it helps to keep them separate before combining them on one graph. A vertical asymptote comes from a zero of the denominator that is not canceled by a matching zero in the numerator; the curve shoots off to positive or negative infinity as x approaches that value. A horizontal asymptote comes from comparing the degrees of the numerator and denominator as x approaches infinity in either direction; if the denominator's degree is larger, the asymptote is y = 0, if the degrees are equal, the asymptote is y equal to the ratio of the leading coefficients, and if the numerator's degree is larger, there is no horizontal asymptote at all. A slant, or oblique, asymptote shows up in that last case specifically when the numerator's degree is exactly one more than the denominator's, and it comes from polynomial division rather than a simple ratio.

Let f(x) = (x^2 + 1)/(x - 1). The domain excludes x = 1. Checking whether that is a real asymptote or a hole: the numerator at x = 1 is 1 + 1 = 2, nonzero, so it is a genuine vertical asymptote. As x approaches 1 from the left, the numerator stays close to 2 (positive) while (x - 1) is a small negative number, so f approaches negative infinity. As x approaches 1 from the right, (x - 1) is a small positive number, so f approaches positive infinity.

The numerator has degree 2 and the denominator has degree 1, so there is no horizontal asymptote, but the degree difference of exactly one signals a slant asymptote. Dividing: x^2 + 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) + 2, which can be checked by expanding (x - 1)(x + 1) = x^2 - 1 and adding 2 to get x^2 + 1 back. So f(x) = x + 1 + 2/(x - 1). As x approaches positive or negative infinity, the remainder term 2/(x - 1) shrinks to zero, so f(x) behaves more and more like the line y = x + 1; that line is the slant asymptote.

It is possible to say even more: does the curve approach that slant line from above or below? Look at the sign of the leftover term, f(x) - (x + 1) = 2/(x - 1). As x approaches positive infinity, x - 1 is a large positive number, so this difference is a small positive number, meaning f(x) is slightly greater than x + 1; the curve sits just above its slant asymptote out to the right. As x approaches negative infinity, x - 1 is a large negative number, so the difference is a small negative number, meaning f(x) is slightly less than x + 1; the curve sits just below its slant asymptote out to the left.

One more case rounds out the horizontal and slant asymptote rules for completeness: if the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's by two or more, there is no horizontal asymptote and no slant asymptote either, since polynomial division leaves a quotient that is itself an unbounded curve rather than a straight line; the graph is not asymptotic to any line at all in that situation, even though it still may have vertical asymptotes wherever the denominator vanishes.
